Just wrapped up my first-ever hackathon (and first-ever hackathon win) at the Roo Code Hackathon 2025! Together with Benjamin Hu , Yifan Wen , and David Javnozon , we built Forklift: an AI-powered web app to make getting started in open-source easier than ever. By cutting onboarding friction, Forklift lets contributors focus on coding and helps projects grow their communities faster. Core features include: - Personalized repo recommendations based on your skills - Concise summaries of a project’s purpose and stack - Smart issue triage with clear difficulty labels (easy / medium / hard) We were honored to win Best First-Time Hack! Check out our project 👉 https://lnkd.in/gX5xUbUT Shoutout to Major League Hacking and Roo Code for putting on an awesome event! #hackathon #AI #opensource #roocode #majorleaguehacking ...more

Dear Spindrift Beverage Co, Inc. , I am writing to you on behalf of our office fridge, and frankly, on behalf of many office fridges in America. Please replace the lemon flavor in the 4-flavor pack. It is consistently neglected, and the subsequent buildup of lemon cans in our office fridge is concerning. Unsettling, even. My team members and I have resorted to drinking one every few days, begrudgingly, as part of our civic duty to reduce lemon spindrift buildup. We are outnumbered by these cans and at risk of coup. Raspberry Lime and Mango Orange go quickly, and Grapefruit is next best. Lemon stays on the shelves, perpetually. Nobody reaches for it on purpose. Please add a replacement flavor (we suggest Fiji Apple or Pineapple). Or perhaps, your team can implement a Spindrift swap service, so we can give our cans away to other offices in exchange for better flavors. We believe there is a market here. The people have spoken. Thank you for your consideration. Evidence attached below.

Palantir Technologies blew my mind this summer. In the first four weeks of my internship, I production-deployed optimizations that cut a key service’s cost and memory usage by more than 10x. After I finished my designated project early, my lead entrusted me with a major refactor of a fleetwide service. I got the chance to do more than just execute; I put together information by collaborating with cross-team stakeholders, created my own scope and went through design review, and mobilized two team members for execution. I’m thankful to my incredible team for being role models and pushing me to excellence. And I really enjoyed working towards the mission while getting to build my skills in distributed systems and optimization. But what really blew me away is the level of trust I was allowed to earn by proving myself. At no point did I feel like “just the intern”; I got to deliver real value in production and my own abilities were the only factor dictating my impact. Back to Pittsburgh. Excited for what’s ahead :)

I'm excited to launch Browser Actions, which extend Decagon agents beyond APIs and into virtually any web application. A lot of the systems our customers depend on every day don't expose APIs. They're internal tools, partner portals, and legacy applications that still require someone to log in and navigate a web interface. Browser Actions solve that by allowing Decagon agents to interact directly with those interfaces, completing complex workflows without a traditional integration. We built Browser Actions on the same secure execution framework that powers the rest of our platform, with isolated browser sessions and full visibility into every action an agent takes. This opens up an entirely new class of workflows for AI agents. See the full launch below.

Super excited that the first episode of our podcast, The Last Mile, is out with Nick Mehta , former CEO of Gainsight ! We talked about the evolution of FDEs, what customer success can teach this new function, and where AI-native services are headed. We also touched on the future of systems integrators. Nick has spent over a decade building one of the defining post-sales companies, so he has a unique perspective on where this market is going. His take: customers will increasingly buy outcomes, not hours. Software is becoming a commodity; services can be a differentiator for customer trust and revenue enablement. Does that mean the time-and-materials model is starting to break? Full episode in the comments.

Just crossed the halfway point of my internship at IBM, and I got the opportunity to work out of the One Madison Avenue office in New York this week. Most of my summer has been at the Silicon Valley Lab in San Jose, building a full stack application that supports IBM's AI assisted mainframe migrations. The part I own is the assessment side, the step where our migration teams scope what a migration would actually take. I build the APIs that turn a client's environment data into that scoped picture, and no two environments look the same, which is most of the problem. Thank you to Jacky Chow for showing me around OMA and for the conversations about tech consulting and client engineering. I came into this summer thinking the job was just writing good code. Those conversations reframed it. The engineers I want to be like understand the client's problem before they open the editor, and that context is what makes the code good in the first place. Only halfway in and I have already learned much. Looking forward to what else I can build and get exposure to before the summer closes. Onwards.

This Wednesday, I had the chance to speak at Women Tech Meetup hosted by Dasha Shunina from OpenRouter , in front of 100+ incredible women in tech. It's always really exciting to see so many women building, founding companies, leading teams, and just being genuinely curious about where AI is going. Communities like this matter a lot, and it's always a pleasure to be part of them. We spent a lot of time talking about AI agents, and I also shared how we're thinking about AI deployments at Contour . One thing I strongly believe is that the hard part isn't building another agent. It's giving that agent the right context. Every deployment creates a huge amount of knowledge: requirements, decisions, stakeholder context, edge cases, what worked, what didn't. Most of it ends up scattered across Slack, docs, tickets, or just stays in people's heads. That's why ontology is such an important piece of the puzzle. It's how you turn all of those implementation learnings into something AI can actually reason over, not just search. I also really loved the questions from the audience. They turned into some of the best conversations of the evening. And apparently there are quite a few WisprFlow fans in the room too haha. Huge thank you to Dasha for the invitation and for creating such a unique atmosphere. Looking forward to the next one <3

Yesterday, Aditya Bankoti , Ioli Shrivastava, Berkan M. va, Berkan M. and I placed 2nd at the Dell × NVIDIA AI Hackathon hosted by BuilderBase. We were given < 10 hours and a GB10 powered computer to build a local solution to any problem. So, we built Nazar... Some places just can't put their data in the cloud. Hospitals, ships, air-gapped banks. So when something breaks, one engineer flies out and stares at logs alone at 2am. We built Nazar, a box that does the staring for them. It reads the broken machines, maps out how everything connects, and a local LLM works the case like a detective until it can tell you what broke and how to fix it. every claim it makes is a footnote pointing at a real line in a real file, so you can check its work. Plugging in an ethernet cable is the entire user interface. And, nothing ever leaves the building.
